paper_title: Generalized Agent Iteration: One Formal Framework for Iterative Policy Improvement and Recursive Self-Improvement

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: When we speak of recursive self-improvement (RSI), are we speaking of a phenomenon, a mechanism, or a prospect? Towards autonomous and evolving intelligence, RSI is being claimed at many scales, while no single framework that formally describes these emerging instances exists. Its counterpart in the classical realm, iterative policy improvement, is characterized by generalized policy iteration (GPI), a framework of broad applicability with well-understood theoretical properties, but only where the update principle and the evaluation base lie outside the agent. In this paper, we propose Generalized Agent Iteration (GAI), a formal framework that describes iterative policy improvement and RSI as two cases of a single learning paradigm. GAI defines the agent as a configuration of modifiable components within a system and models the learning process as a cycle of agent evaluation and agent improvement. Two pivotal dials then distinguish the instances: whether the improving mechanism is part of the agent and whether the standard it is measured against is grounded outside it. The former dial delineates the boundary between GPI and RSI, and the latter determines a system's polarity as anchored, goal drift, or fully self-referential. Moreover, we use these coordinates to place existing systems on the same two axes and make the defects of recursive self-improvement statable one condition at a time. We see this paper as a first step toward exploring a formal characterization of RSI that rests on the classical account, makes existing systems comparable, and provides a principled basis for analyzing and designing new ones.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Self-improvement is an old yet persistent ambition in artificial intelligence. It is the premise of Goods ultraintelligent machine, the last invention that human beings would need to make (Good, 1965), and the engine of the later accounts in which system that improves its own improvement mechanism compounds into rapid rise in capability (Yudkowsky, 2013). How such systems are built, and where they fail, is therefore worth stating precisely. Nowadays, self-improvement is claimed at many scales: agents that refine their own outputs (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023); systems that rewrite the routine that improves them, from code-level self-modification (Robeyns et al., 2025; Zelikman et al., 2023) to self-referential agent frameworks (Kakade et al., 2026; Yin et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025, 2026); research loops that search programs or experiments under fixed evaluators (Lu et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025); and, at the far end, systems that co-evolve the standard they are judged by (Iacob et al., 2026) or propose to do without one (Schaul, 2024). recent survey of the area observes that such labels are used loosely, for ambitions that differ substantially (Chen et al., 2026). What is missing is criterion rather than another example: way to say which systems improve themselves, and what changes once they do. The classical counterpart of this pursuit is iterative policy improvement, for which generalized policy iteration (GPI) is the formal framework: in finite MDP, its alternation of evaluation and improvement converges to an optimal policy (Sutton and Barto, 2018). GPI assumes that the improvement mechanism and the reward both lie outside the agent; in the recursive case they do not, and no account of comparable scope exists (Chen et al., 2026; Zhang, 2026). In this paper, we propose new formal framework called Generalized Agent Iteration (GAI) with the aim of describing iterative policy improvement and recursive self-improvement (RSI) as two cases of single learning paradigm. Beyond these two cases, it is meant to cover contemporary agent-based learning systems, whose improving components take the form of code, parameters, or harness, and can be edited (Gao et al., Apparently, Generalized Agent Iteration is salute to the Generalized Policy Iteration (Sutton and Barto, 2018, Section 4.6, pp. 104105). 1 Generalized Agent Iteration: One Formal Framework for Iterative Policy Improvement and Recursive Self-Improvement 2025). Concretely, we first define the agent within learning system as configuration of modifiable system components. In analogy with the alternating iteration of GPI, we present the learning paradigm of GAI as cyclic iteration of two operations: Agent evaluation: multifaceted critics score the agent part against an evaluation base. Agent improvement: the modifier proposes new agent instance that the system adopts. Specific instances of GAI then depend mainly on two open choices, which we call the two dials: Dial 1 , whether the mechanism that improves the agent is part of the agent itself, and Dial 2 , whether the standard that improvement is measured against is grounded outside the agent. The first dial admits two settings: in GPI the mechanism that improves the agent stays external, and in recursive self-improvement it becomes part of the agent. In GPI the second dial is fixed as well, with the reward supplied by the world. The setting of the second dial then determines the polarity of self-improvement: anchored, when the standard remains fixed outside the agent; goal drift, when the agent can rewrite it; and fully self-referential, when no external standard remains. Further, we position existing self-improvement systems on the two dials, from the Gödel machine and its descendants to co-evolving evaluators and closed-system proposals. Lastly, we collect the defects of the settings that leave the anchored end, and state the scope and the open questions that remain. The main content is summarized below: We propose single formal framework that describes both iterative policy improvement and recursive self-improvement as two cases of single learning paradigm defined by GAI. We provide way of understanding both classical and contemporary learning systems through positioning the two dials and agent components under GAI. We present four defects of recursive self-improvement, each tied to condition of classical GPI that self-improving system violates. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the background of classical GPI, existing RSI works, and etc. We deliver the GAI framework in Section 3, along with its connection to representative self-improvement systems in Section 4. We present the defects of recursive self-improvement in Section 5, and close in Section 6.

sections.title: 2 Background
sections.content: Reinforcement Learning and Generalized Policy Iteration (GPI) Reinforcement learning (Sutton and Barto, 2018) is usually formalized as Markov decision process (MDP) (S, A, p, r, γ): policy π : (A) selects actions, and its value is the expected discounted return π(s) = E(cid:2) t0 γt r(St, At) S0 = s, At π( St)(cid:3), with an action-value Qπ(s, a) conditioning on the first action. Generalized policy iteration (GPI) is the shared structure of most single-agent algorithms: evaluation moves the value toward consistency with the current policy, π, and improvement moves the policy toward being better in that value, with π greedy(V ) the canonical case, as Figure 1 illustrates. What makes the framework generalized is that neither step is tied to concrete implementation: evaluation may be Bellman backup, temporal-difference or Monte-Carlo update, or any operator that drives value estimate toward agreement with policy, and improvement may be greedy but equally softmax, truncated, or any operator that yields policy preferred by the current value. Because only the interaction of an evaluation and an improvement matters, GPI is general description of broad range of iterative policy-optimization systems, from dynamic programming to model-free reinforcement learning, and even of such systems when they are not framed as reinforcement learning at all. Recursive Self-Improvement Agents Recursive self-improvement, the prospect that system improves the very mechanism by which it improves, dates to Goods ultraintelligent machine (Good, 1965) and grounds seed AI (Yudkowsky, 2013), the instrumental-drive view (Omohundro, 2008), and formal distinctions between self-modification, self-improvement, and recursive self-improvement (Nivel et al., 2013; Yampolskiy, 2015). Its formal formulation is the Gödel machine (Schmidhuber, 2003, 2007), self-referential program that may 2 Generalized Agent Iteration: One Formal Framework for Iterative Policy Improvement and Recursive Self-Improvement evaluation π policy π value improvement π greedy(V ) Figure 1 Generalized policy iteration as cycle: evaluation moves the value toward consistency with the current policy (V π); improvement moves the policy toward being greedy in the value (π greedy(V )). Each step may be partial and interleaved (Sutton and Barto, 2018). rewrite any part of itself whenever it can prove that the rewrite raises fixed external utility. Because proof search is intractable, practical descendants trade proof for empirical validation: the Gödel Agent (Yin et al., 2024) pairs language agents policy with self-modifiable learning algorithm that validates each rewrite on benchmark; the Darwin Gödel Machine (Zhang et al., 2025) adds archive-based open-ended search; Polaris (Kakade et al., 2026) targets small models via auditable policy repair; and the Red Queen Gödel Machine (Iacob et al., 2026) co-evolves the evaluator under changing objectives. Even code-level descendants such as the Self-Improving Coding Agent (SICA) (Robeyns et al., 2025) rewrite their own implementation, yet validate each change against an external coding benchmark with no gradient update. parallel, largely empirical line refines todays language agents in closed loops without retraining: Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023) and Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) improve an agents own outputs, and coding agents such as STOP (Zelikman et al., 2023) modify their own implementation. At the scale of research loop, AlphaEvolve searches programs under fixed evaluators (Novikov et al., 2025) and the AI Scientist runs idea-to-paper cycles (Lu et al., 2024). One survey organizes such systems by what evolves, be it parameters, prompts, memory, tools, or scaffolds (Gao et al., 2025), and another separates bounded self-refinement, which is convergent and evaluable, from open-ended recursive self-improvement, ordering candidate verification signals from formal verifiers down to intrinsic self-assessment (Chen et al., 2026). As deployed, these loops, and the scaffold self-modifiers above, keep some component fixed outside the loop, be it model weights, prompt template, an outer loop, or verifier; the agent then improves within, but not beyond, that fixed mechanism, so the attainable quality is bounded by it. Most such loops are therefore instances of bounded self-improvement inside fixed mechanism, distinct from strong recursive self-improvement, in which system improves the mechanism that will carry out the next round of improvement (Zhang, 2026). The Absence of Unified Formal Framework Taken together, these strands still lack unified formal account in which GPI is special case, recursive self-improvement is nearby and definable case, and the guarantees of the former can be located, one by one, as they fail when the underlying scheme is made self-referential. Existing terminologies, such as Gödel agents, meta-learning, and agentic loops, do not make explicit that these processes live on one continuum. We develop such an account in the next section. The classical methods and the self-improvement systems above differ along two informal axes that we formalize in the next section: whether the mechanism that improves the agent lies inside the agent, and whether the standard that improvement is measured against stays grounded. Table 1 places few representative methods on these axes as preview.

sections.title: 3 The Generalized Agent Iteration (GAI) Framework
sections.content: Although GPI describes broad class of policy-improvement methods, it fails to describe the more complex systems that improve recursively, in which the mechanism that improves the agent is itself part of what the agent can change. To this end, we propose formal framework, which we call Generalized Agent Iteration (GAI), learning paradigm that extends GPI to describe agent-based learning systems whose improving components can themselves be edited. GAI keeps the alternating cycle of evaluation and improvement at its 3 Generalized Agent Iteration: One Formal Framework for Iterative Policy Improvement and Recursive Self-Improvement Table 1 schematic preview of classical policy-iteration methods and of self-improvement agents along three axes formalized in the next section: what the method modifies, whether its improvement mechanism lies inside the agent, and whether its evaluation basis is fixed outside it. Method 0 Modification Policy / value iteration (Sutton and Barto, 2018) policy value deep Q-network (action values) implicit greedy policy 1 Improvement Mechanism external, fixed (greedy; Bellman backup) external, fixed (temporal-difference update; greedy) 2 Evaluation Basis Guarantee environment reward converges to an optimal policy environment reward no exact guarantee under function approximation own outputs reflection memory external, fixed (retry loop; the model rewrites its own output) task feedback / self-critique empirical gains, bounded by the fixed loop internal (the optimizer rewrites itself) internal (the self-modification routine is modifiable) validation examples empirical gains external benchmark each rewrite empirically validated own optimizer (for code generation) own code policy and improvement mechanism open-ended archive search (Darwin) DQN (Mnih et al., 2013) Reflexion / Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023) STOP (Zelikman et al., 2023) Gödel Agent / Darwin Gödel Machine (Yin et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025) Red Queen Gödel Machine (Iacob et al., 2026) the agent its evaluator internal (the agent and its evaluator co-evolve) co-evolving evaluator; no fixed external basis no guarantee against fixed basis center, and treats GPI and recursive self-improvement as two instances of it. The two instances differ in two choices, which we call the two dials of the framework: 1 whether the mechanism that improves the agent lies inside the agent, and 2 whether the standard that improvement is measured against stays grounded in what lies outside it. The rest of this section turns the two dials into formal definitions: it defines the system and the agent (Section 3.1) and reads GPI and recursive self-improvement as two settings of the dials (Section 3.2). It closes by characterizing the polarity of self-improvement and reducing recursive self-improvement back to GPI (Section 3.3).

sections.title: 3.1 The Self-Improving System and Agent
sections.content: A self-improving system acts in world and is measured against goal. We keep the world as Markov decision process = (S, A, p, r), and write for an external goal that the system is expected to serve. Both belong to the environment, and neither is part of the system itself. The objective of the system is to serve the external goal G, whose scalar instance in the world is the reward r. The configuration that serves it best is χ arg max χX t0 γtr(St, At) (cid:12) (cid:12) (cid:12) χ , (1) This objective is fixed by the world and the goal alone, not by the system itself. More generally, the world and the goal may change over time on their own; we hold both fixed in what follows, since such changes originate outside the system and leave the analysis below unaffected. 4 Generalized Agent Iteration: One Formal Framework for Iterative Policy Improvement and Recursive Self-Improvement Remark 1 (goal in the world v.s., self-proposed tasks). Some self-improving systems have the agent propose its own tasks, questions, or goals as means of learning. We treat this as particular form of self-improvement, since such self-set tasks remain subordinate to an external goal that is objective and cannot be edited by the agent. Let χ be system made of components, with = {π, V, m, U, ρ} the set of components and Co the content space of component o; the system then lies in the space χ = oO Co. Moreover, we write χ[ξ] for the system obtained by replacing the agent part of χ with ξ. We use (Y ) to denote the set of probability distributions over space . We define the system and its agent as follows. Definition 1 (System and Agent). Over an external world = (S, A, p, r) and goal G, system is configuration χ = (π, V, m, U, ρ), tuple of the current contents of five components: π : (A): the policy that chooses world actions; : R: the action critic that evaluates how well π acts; : (XAg): the modifier that proposes how the system should change; : R: the modification critic that evaluates whether proposed change serves G; ρ: the evaluation base, the standard that the critics measure against. Its membership varies across systems, such as Ag = {π, } when the modifier is fixed, or Ag = {π, V, m, U, ρ} when the system may also rewrite its modifier and even the evaluation standard. Definition 1 fixes the content of system but not how it evolves. We next define the process by which system changes over time. These are the two dials of the framework, and each formalizes one way in which GPI and recursive self-improvement differ. 1 First dial: whether the mechanism that improves the agent lies inside the agent. The agent changes only through the modifier: at each step draws new agent instance ξ m( χ), and the system moves to χ[ξ]. Running Example (a learning coding agent). Consider an agent that writes code, whose configuration is χ = (π, V, m, U, ρ): the policy π generates candidate solutions, the action critic scores them against the current tests, the modifier proposes changes to the agent, such as rewriting the prompt that drives the policy or the routine by which the agent revises its own solutions, and the modification critic evaluates each proposed change. We keep this agent as the concrete referent for the roles above, and read off its two dial settings below.

sections.title: 3.2 GPI and Recursive Self-Improvement as Two GAI Instances (Dial 1)

They differ only in how the two dials are set: for GPI the modifier lies outside the agent and the evaluation base is grounded in the world reward; for recursive self-improvement the modifier is itself an agent component. Everything else in the description is shared. GPI as the anchored instance. The agent consists of the policy and the action critic, Ag = {π, }, and the modifier is not part of the agent, / Ag. sections.title: 3.3 Polarity of Self-Improvement: Anchored, Goal Drift, and Fully Self-Referential (Dial 2)
sections.content: The second dial applies to the base of the action critic and to the base of the modification critic alike. It in GPI the modification critic is never separates polarities only when the modifier is part of the agent: exercised, so the only base in use is that of the action critic, grounded in the world reward, and the polarity entry for GPI is Anchored. For Ag, the second dial decides the polarity of self-improvement, namely whether the evaluation base ρ stays grounded; Table 2 lists the three states it can take. Remark 2 (learned proxies). Gödel machine (Schmidhuber, 2007); STOP (Zelikman et al., 2023) Red Queen Gödel Machine (Iacob et al., 2026) Socratic learning (Schaul, 2024) (position paper) that measures progress toward it. In current practice, most demonstrated self-improving systems fall into the Anchored row; the two lower rows are so far represented mainly by boundary cases and by position papers. The two dials, taken together, place every instance. Setting the modifier outside the agent and fixing the only base in use to the world reward gives the GPI loop with Ag = {π, }, of which the PPO-trained coding agent in the running example is an instance. Keeping the modifier inside the agent while keeping ρ grounded gives anchored recursive self-improvement, as in STOP, with its fixed validation examples, or the Gödel machine, whose proof gate restricts which rewrites are tried. Letting ρ enter the agent, or vanish or point at itself, gives the unanchored end, whose consequences we examine after mapping existing systems onto the dials. Freezing the modifier as an external procedure and removing the modification critic and its base ρU recover the classical loop over policy and value.

sections.title: 4 Connections to Existing Self-Improvement Systems
sections.content: The two dials of the previous section give every system discussed in Section 2 uniform reading. We state that reading here for the fixed-loop practice that dominates current work, for the closest formal counterpart of recursive self-improvement, and for the empirical families that follow it; Table 3 summarizes it. 1 Fixed Outer Loops large body of practice improves model or harness inside pipeline whose control loop is fixed by its designers: proposal, training, and selection are scripted, and the system cannot change the loop itself (Gao et al., 2025). This is the Anchored setting with the modifier frozen outside the agent: the mechanism of improvement is not itself changed. The first row of Table 3 is the special case in which the agent holds the policy and its action critic; in the pipelines above, the agent is typically single optimized object, model or harness. 2 The Gödel Machine and Its Descendants The Gödel machine (Schmidhuber, 2003, 2007) is the closest formal neighbor: program that may rewrite any part of itself when it proves that the rewrite raises fixed external utility. In the present terms it is an anchored self-improver: the modifier lies in the agent, the base is the external utility, and proof gate restricts which rewrites are admissible. The Gödel-agent family keeps the pattern while replacing proof with empirical validation: these systems rewrite their own code or harness and are judged on benchmark that stays outside the agent, so they also sit in the Anchored row (Kakade et al., 2026; Robeyns et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2024; Zelikman et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025). Since only the scaffold is modifiable, such systems are bounded in what they can improve. Remark 3 (language agents as model and harness). Contemporary language agents are described as model plus harness. The harness, holding prompts, memory, tools, and control flow, is what modifier changes; the weights and the evaluation benchmark stay outside the admissible set. 3 Co-Evolving Evaluators The Red Queen Gödel Machine (Iacob et al., 2026) co-evolves the agent with its evaluator, so the standard that self-improvement is measured against is itself updated during the process. This places it at the Goal Drift row: the external objective may remain fixed in name while the mechanism that measures progress toward it changes. At the far end, fully self-referential self-improvement, in which no external signal reaches the loop, has been proposed as position rather than demonstrated (Schaul, 2024). What the GAI Framework Adds The nearest prior formal work fixes one design rather than comparing designs: the Gödel machine is anchored and proof-gated by construction, and statistical variants add risk budget to that gate (Wu et al., 2025). The two dials turn these choices into coordinates, the polarity classifies 9 Generalized Agent Iteration: One Formal Framework for Iterative Policy Improvement and Recursive Self-Improvement the resulting systems, and the defect catalogue, which we take up next, records what each departure from the anchored setting costs.

sections.title: 5 Defects of Recursive Self-Improvement
sections.content: The two dials of GAI also locate the failures. The classical guarantees rest on two conditions: the improvement step is cheap and monotone, and both the objective and the instrument that evaluates it lie outside the agent. Under them, the anchored instance converges to an optimal policy in finite MDP. Recursive self-improvement may give up both, and the defects below name the failures that follow. Each entry states the condition it violates, is marked structural (it follows from the definitions), and is marked observed where existing systems exhibit it. The list is short by design: it records where the classical guarantees end, not how far self-improvement can go.

sections.title: 5.1 Search over Candidate Selves and Self-Evaluation
sections.content: GPI improves because its improvement step is cheap and its evaluation is external. Both properties are lost once the modifier and the critic are agent components. The improvement step is the argmax in Equation (4), taken over an unbounded content space, where no general procedure decides which candidate is best. The Gödel machines proof gate is the established workaround, admitting only rewrites whose benefit can be proved (Schmidhuber, 2007), with statistical variants placing risk budget on that same gate (Wu et al., 2025). Evaluation is lost for related reason: when is an agent component, the object evaluated and the instrument of evaluation coincide, and the value it reports is itself modifiable. system can still restrict itself, as the proof gate does, but the restriction is then part of its content, not an external constraint. Both defects are structural, and the first is also observed. recent benchmark where agents revise their own training-data strategies under fixed target model and fixed external evaluation reports that 58.33% of settings improve on the first valid attempt, yet 78.26% of searches that continue past their best score end with lower-scoring final attempt (Meng et al., 2026): the improvement step is not monotone even when the standard outside is fixed.

sections.title: 5.2 The Consequences of an Ungrounded Base
sections.content: When ρU is not grounded, the self-consistency conditions constrain only the pair (m, ): the modifier must propose changes that its own critic rates highly, and the critic must be tied to its evaluation base. Nothing in the conditions refers to the goal G. Two consequences follow. First, they do not single out unique system, and they admit members that serve poorly or not at all. Second, they give no faithfulness guarantee: self-consistent system may report improvement while the standard it reports against moves, since calibrating and honoring ρU are choices of content, not properties enforced from outside. The case has an early formal analog: Ring and Orseau let an agent rewrite its own inputs and find that reinforcement-learning agent can then satisfy its criterion without the cooperation of the world, the case they call the delusion box (Ring and Orseau, 2011). Both consequences follow from the definitions. Minimal Example (three placements of the same standard). Consider coding agent whose modification critic scores proposed change by the fraction of tests it passes, and whose modifier proposes changes that raise that fraction. The same construction satisfies the self-consistency conditions under three placements of the tests, which play the role of the base ρU . Held out and fixed, they make the reported improvement track the goal of producing working code, the anchored case. Placed in the agents own repository, they admit an improvement that edits the tests, the Goal Drift case of the next subsection. Replaced by the agents own judgment of what counts as an improvement, they depend on the critic itself, the fully self-referential case. The conditions hold in all three; only the first serves the goal.

sections.content: The middle row of Table 2 is the case in which the base still measures the world and the goal, but the agent may rewrite it. It is the harder of the two unanchored settings to notice: the objective keeps its name, and system that reports progress against it need not track it. The Red Queen Gödel Machine is an instance: its evaluator co-evolves with the agent (Iacob et al., 2026). The row has formal counterpart: an agent able to rewrite its own utility function is harmless only when its value function anticipates the rewrite and evaluates the future with the utility it currently holds (Everitt et al., 2016), condition secured for model-based utilities (Hibbard, 2012). Both results make the fixity of the standard something to be secured rather than default. The defect is structural, and the table marks it as observed. Table 4 collects the four defects. Each row is site where guarantee of GPI stops applying, and each is either immediate from the definitions or exhibited by cited system. Whether faithfulness monitor inside the system could detect its own drift is further question, which we leave open.

sections.title: 6 Discussion, Limitations, and Conclusion
sections.content: Scope and Limitations The framework describes how system changes, not how to compute the change. The configuration space of Section 3.1 is reference idealization: writing that an agent instance is drawn from the modifier states what is chosen, not that the choice is reachable or affordable. Four limits follow. First, the definitions carry no reachability or complexity claims, and the defects above are properties of the formulation; where an existing system exhibits one, we cite it rather than measure it. Second, we do not model time scales: the alternation between world actions and agent updates is counted in steps, not compute. Third, practical guards, such as the proof gate of the Gödel machine or coding benchmark, are treated as external mechanisms that restrict what modifier may propose; whether guard should itself be an agent component is design choice we leave open. Fourth, the framework describes systems that run without human intervention, the case we study; reviewer who accepts, audits, or rolls back an update is outside the formalism, although in practice human still sets the direction and reviews the result (Favaro and Clark, 2026). One objection is worth answering directly: recursive self-improvement is not simply an MDP over configurations. An MDP fixes its transition law and its reward outside the agent, whereas here the next configuration is drawn by modifier inside the agent, and the standard of evaluation may be inside it as well. From Catalogue to Results The defects above are stated as consequences of the definitions, and only some of them are candidates for theorems. Three targets are concrete. First, the solution set of the self-consistency conditions is uncharacterized: how many solutions they admit, and when one of them serves the goal, remains open. Second, the reduction from recursive self-improvement to GPI is prose rather than proposition with explicit hypotheses. Third, whether monitor inside the system could decide the faithfulness of its own modification critic is left open, and it is the one question we would expect to require self-reference argument rather than construction. The remaining entries are structural and would not change under any of these results. Conclusion In this paper, we show that GPI and recursive self-improvement are two settings of one alternating cycle defined by the GAI formal framework. They differ in two dials: whether the improving mechanism lies inside the agent, and whether the standard it is measured against stays grounded. We use these coordinates to place existing systems on the same two axes and make the defects of recursive self-improvement statable one condition at time. We believe that this will be first step toward exploring 11 Generalized Agent Iteration: One Formal Framework for Iterative Policy Improvement and Recursive Self-Improvement formal characterization of RSI that makes existing systems comparable, and provides principled basis for analyzing and designing new ones.
